question: My opponent shouted 'fault!' while I was playing my shot. What's the ruling?

answer.reasoning: The question asks what happens when the opponent shouts 'fault!' while you are playing your shot. itto-5.9.1.4 directly covers a player calling 'fault' to the opponent when making a stroke or after the opponent has made a stroke, classifying it as deliberate distraction under Law 13.4.5. laws-13.4.5 makes deliberate distraction by shouting a fault under Law 13.4 when in play. laws-7.3 gives the consequence: the side wins the rally if the opposing side commits a fault, and the side winning a rally adds a point. itto-5.9.1.3 (shouting to a partner) does not apply because the shout was directed at the opponent, not a partner. All parts are covered.
answer.answer: Your opponent's shout of 'fault!' while you were making your stroke is a fault against your opponent. The Instructions to Technical Officials 7.0 (5) state that "A player calling 'fault', etc. to the opponent when making a stroke or after the opponent has made a stroke, shall be considered a deliberate distraction (Law 13.4.5)" [itto-5.9.1.4], and the Laws of Badminton 5.0 (2) provide that under Law 13.4 it is a fault "if, in play, a player: deliberately distracts an opponent by any action such as shouting or making gestures" [laws-13.4.5]. Because your opponent committed a fault, you win the rally: "A side shall win a rally, if the opposing side commits a 'fault'" and "The side winning a rally shall add a point to its score" [laws-7.3], so the ruling is a fault against your opponent and a point to you.

question: When do we replay a rally? List every situation that counts as a let.

answer.reasoning: The question has two parts: (1) when a rally is replayed — answered by Law 14.3 (effect of a let) and Law 14.1 (who calls a let), both in Laws of Badminton 5.0 (2); (2) every situation that counts as a let — answered by Law 14.2 and its sub-clauses 14.2.1–14.2.7, with 14.2.3 expanded by 14.2.3.1 and 14.2.3.2 (the parent lead-in 'after the service is returned, the shuttle is:' is cited with each child). Searches confirmed no further 14.2.x clauses exist. The ITTO 7.0 (5) clause 5.9.1.2 adds the adjacent-court shuttle qualification. All parts are covered; nothing is missing.
answer.answer:
A rally is replayed whenever a "let" is called. Under the Laws of Badminton 5.0 (2), in force 2025-04-26, Law 14.1: "‘Let’ shall be called by the umpire, or by a player (if there is no umpire), to halt play." When a let occurs, Law 14.3: "When a ‘let’ occurs, play since the last service shall not count and the player who served last shall serve again." — so the rally since the last service does not count and is replayed by the player who served last.

Law 14.2 of the same Laws lists every situation that is a let:
1. "the server serves before the receiver is ready (Law 9.4);" (Clause 14.2.1)
2. "during service, the receiver and the server are both faulted;" (Clause 14.2.2)
3. "after the service is returned, the shuttle is:" (Clause 14.2.3) — either "caught on the net and remains suspended on its top;" (Clause 14.2.3.1) or "after passing over the net is caught in the net;" (Clause 14.2.3.2)
4. "during play, the shuttle disintegrates and the base completely separates from the rest of the shuttle;" (Clause 14.2.4)
5. "in the opinion of the umpire, play is disrupted or a player of the opposing side is distracted by a coach;" (Clause 14.2.5)
6. "a line judge is unsighted and the umpire or Instant Review System is unable to make a decision; or" (Clause 14.2.6)
7. "any unforeseen or accidental situation has occurred." (Clause 14.2.7)

One qualification from the Instructions to Technical Officials 7.0 (5), in force 2025-04-26, Clause 5.9.1.2: "A shuttle coming onto the court from an adjacent court shall not automatically be considered a “let”. A “let” shall not be called in such circumstances if, in the opinion of the Umpire, the shuttle has not obstructed or distracted the players;"

question: My partner cut his hand mid-game and it's bleeding. How long can we stop, and who can come on court to help?

answer.reasoning: The question has two parts: (1) how long play may stop for a bleeding cut, and (2) who may come on court to help. Both are covered by the Instructions to Technical Officials 7.0 (5), in force 2025-04-26. Part 1: itto-5.14.2 sets the delay for a blood-flowing injury (until bleeding stops, wound dressed, or Referee advises otherwise); itto-3.6.1.4 requires the Referee to resolve it as quickly as possible and well within a few minutes, with potential disqualification if the injury is exploited; itto-5.14.1 bars treatment causing undue delay on court and has the Umpire time the delay; itto-3.6.1.2 allows the Tournament Doctor only quick relief such as a bandage, with no time-consuming treatment except in regular intervals. Part 2: itto-3.6.1.3 allows a maximum of two persons on court to assist and advise the injured player and help with translation, with the same consideration for the opposing side; itto-3.6.1.1 has the Referee and Tournament Doctor go on court immediately when called; itto-5.14.1 has the Referee decide whether the Tournament Doctor or anyone else is required on court. No part is missing, so refused is false.
answer.answer: How long you can stop: for a blood-flowing injury, the game should be delayed until the bleeding stops, the wound is suitably dressed, or the Referee advises the Umpire otherwise (Instructions to Technical Officials 7.0 (5), in force 2025-04-26, Clause 5.14.2). The Referee shall resolve the injury situation as quickly as possible and well within a few minutes so that play can be resumed or abandoned, and the Referee may point to potential disqualification against your side if it is suspected that your partner is exploiting the injury situation to regain wind or repeatedly hesitates in deciding to continue or abandon play (Clause 3.6.1.4). No treatment causing undue delay shall be given on court, and the Umpire shall time the delay caused by the injury (Clause 5.14.1). The Tournament Doctor may apply a quick relief to your partner, such as a bandage on a bleeding injury, but no time-consuming treatment is allowed except in the regular intervals and then only if the Tournament Doctor estimates that the treatment can be completed (or nearly so) before the interval ends (Clause 3.6.1.2). Who can come on court: when the Umpire calls in case of injury, the Referee and the Tournament Doctor shall immediately go on court (Clause 3.6.1.1), and the Referee will decide whether the Tournament Doctor or anyone else is required on court (Clause 5.14.1). The Referee may allow a maximum of two persons on court to assist and advise your injured partner and help with translation, and in fairness the Referee shall allow your opponents the same consideration (Clause 3.6.1.3).

citations.quote: For a blood flowing injury, the game should be delayed until the bleeding stops, the wound is suitably dressed, or the Referee advises the Umpire otherwise.

The Referee shall resolve the injury situation as quickly as possible and well within a few minutes so that play can be resumed or abandoned. The Referee may need to point to potential disqualification if it is suspected that the player is exploiting the injury situation to regain wind, or if the player repeatedly hesitates in deciding to continue or abandon play.

The Referee will decide whether the Tournament Doctor or anyone else is required on court (Instruction 3.6). The Tournament Doctor shall examine the player and advise the player about the severity of injury or sickness. No treatment causing undue delay shall be given on court. The Umpire shall time the delay caused by the injury.

The Tournament Doctor may apply a quick relief, such as a bandage on a bleeding injury, but no time-consuming treatment is allowed except in the regular intervals and then only if the Tournament Doctor estimates that the treatment can be completed (or nearly so) before the interval ends.
When called by the Umpire in case of injury or illness, the Referee and the Tournament Doctor shall immediately go on court.

The Referee may allow a maximum of two persons on court to assist and advise the injured player and help with translation. In fairness, the Referee shall allow the opposing side the same consideration.

question: Water started dripping from the roof onto our court mid-game. What happens to the match and the score?

answer.reasoning: The question has two parts: what happens to the match when water makes the court unplayable mid-game, and what happens to the score. itto-5.11.3 and laws-16.3.1 cover suspension of the match; itto-5.11.4 covers the umpire's suspension call; laws-16.3.3 covers the score standing; itto-5.11.5 covers resumption. No part is missing.
answer.answer: Under the Instructions to Technical Officials 7.0 (5), in force 2025-04-26, water dripping onto the court makes it a case where “a court or its immediate surroundings needs repair, or it is temporarily not playable,” so “the Umpire shall call the Referee (or the Referee shall go onto the court) and play be suspended until the court and its immediate surroundings are again suitable for play.” Under the Laws of Badminton 5.0 (2), in force 2025-04-26, “When necessitated by circumstances not within the control of the players, the umpire may suspend play for such a period as the umpire may consider necessary.” When play is suspended, “the Umpire shall call: “Play is suspended” and note “S” on the scoring device or score-sheet, if used.” For you and your opponent, the score does not change: “If play is suspended, the existing score shall stand and play shall be resumed from that point.” When play resumes, “the Umpire shall note the duration of the suspension and ensure that the players are on the correct side of the net and in the correct service courts, then call “Are you ready?” followed by the score and “Play”.

citations.quote: If, during a match, a court or its immediate surroundings needs repair, or it is temporarily not playable, the Umpire shall call the Referee (or the Referee shall go onto the court) and play be suspended until the court and its immediate surroundings are again suitable for play.

question: The line judge couldn't see whether the shuttle landed in. What happens to the rally?

answer.reasoning: The question asks what happens to the rally when the line judge is unsighted. Sources found: itto-8.5 (line judge's unsighted signal), itto-5.8.3 with children 5.8.3.1–5.8.3.3 (umpire's immediate calls where a line judge is unsighted, including the IRS exception), itto-2.5 (umpire makes the decision when another official is unsighted; let if no decision; IRS if in use), and laws-14.2.6 (a let if a line judge is unsighted and the umpire or IRS cannot decide). Together these answer the question fully; no part is missing.
answer.answer: The line judge must inform the Umpire immediately by putting both hands up to cover the eyes (Instructions to Technical Officials 7.0 (5), in force 2025-04-26, Clause 8.5: "If unsighted, inform the Umpire immediately by putting both hands up to cover the eyes."). The Umpire then makes the decision for the rally: where a Line Judge is unsighted, the Umpire shall immediately call "Out" when the shuttle lands outside the line, and then call either the score or "Service over" and then the score (Clause 5.8.3.1: "“Out” when the shuttle lands outside the line and then call either the score or “Service over” and then the score; or"), or call the score or "Service over" and then the score when the shuttle lands "in" (Clause 5.8.3.2: "The score or “Service over” and then the score when the shuttle lands “in”; or"). If the Umpire is also unsighted, the Umpire calls "Let" followed by the score, except when an Instant Review System is in operation, in which case the Umpire calls "Unsighted" and requests a decision from the system by raising the left hand above the head (Clause 5.8.3.3: "“Let” followed by the score when the Umpire is unsighted, except when an IRS is in operation, the Umpire shall call “Unsighted” and request a decision from the system by raising the left hand above the head."). More generally, when another official is unsighted the Umpire shall make the decision, and when no decision can be made a 'let' shall be called, unless IRS is in use, in which case it will be used to decide on the line call (Clause 2.5: "When another official is unsighted, the Umpire shall make the decision. When no decision can be made, a 'let' shall be called (Law 17.6.6), unless IRS is in use, in which case it will be used to decide on the line call (BWF Statutes, Section 4.1.8, Regulation 1.2)."). Under the Laws of Badminton 5.0 (2), in force 2025-04-26, it is a "let" if "a line judge is unsighted and the umpire or Instant Review System is unable to make a decision" (Clause 14.2.6: "a line judge is unsighted and the umpire or Instant Review System is unable to make a decision; or"). So the rally is decided by the Umpire (or the IRS where in operation), and only if neither can decide is the rally replayed as a let.

question: Can my coach get up from his chair and stand at the side of the court during the match?

answer.answer: No. Under the Instructions to Technical Officials 7.0 (5), in force 2025-04-26, "Coaches must be seated in their designated seats and must not stand court-side during the match except during the permitted intervals (Law 16.2)." The only exceptions are the permitted intervals under the Laws of Badminton 5.0 (2), in force 2025-04-26: "not exceeding 60 seconds during each game when the leading score reaches 11 points, except Handicap matches" and "not exceeding 120 seconds between the first and second game, and between the second and third game". So your coach may stand court-side only during those intervals, not during play.

Under Instructions to Technical Officials 7.0 (5), Clause 5.17.10 (in force 2025-04-26), misconduct before the match while on the Field of Play before "Play" has been called is treated as in Instructions 5.17.3, 5.17.4 or 5.17.5, and "Any card(s) given shall have no effect on the score of the match but a card(s) shall be taken into account if further offences occur during the match (Law 16.7.1.2)" — meaning that if your opponent commits a further offence during the match, the umpire faults the offending side "if previously warned" (Laws of Badminton 5.0 (2), Clause 16.7.1.2, in force 2025-04-26). The yellow card itself is a warning for misconduct (Instructions 5.17.3). As for after the tournament: under Instructions to Technical Officials 7.0 (5), Clause 3.7.3 (in force 2025-04-26), "The Referee shall immediately after the tournament send to BWF (or CC) a report on withdrawals, yellow and red cards, that may trigger further sanctions" — so the yellow card is reported to BWF (or CC) after the tournament and may trigger further sanctions against your opponent. The sources do not say anything further about a permanent record beyond this report and possible further sanctions.
